0. Input

Program:

int[] a = {2, 4, 6};
int sum = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
    sum += a[i];
}
System.out.println("Total: " + sum);

Question: Explain how the loop computes the total, and what would change if a fourth element, 8, were added.

Student's answer: The loop visits each index from 0 to a.length - 1 and adds that element to sum, so it prints Total: 12. With 8 added, a.length becomes 4, so the loop runs once more and prints Total: 20, with no other change to the code Settings: width 3, depth 3, prune llm, backend claude-cli, model claude-opus-5-5

Inconsistent application: on some passes the update is applied before the body, or a[i] is traced with the previous i. (here mixing in: "a = a + b adds the arrays element by element") | | lvl:array_traversal@L1#0 | level L1 way names_the_element: Identity: a traversal is a loop that steps an index through the array and performs the same operation on each element it visits. | | lvl:array_traversal@L1#1 | level L1 way states_the_rule: Declarative: the canonical traversal is 'for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { ... a[i] ... }', which gives i every valid index exactly once, in increasing order; the for loop is equivalent to initialize; while (test) { body; increment; }. | | lvl:array_traversal@L2#0 | level L2 way line_by_line_trace: Sequencing: i = 0; test i < a.length; body using a[i]; i++; test; ... for_loop, misconceptions: 21 edges offered

Edges offered: | edge | |---| | err:for_loop->BracelessMultiStatementBody | wrong rule: Indenting several statements under an if or for makes them all part of its body, even without braces. | right rule: Without braces only the first statement belongs to the if/for; the rest run once, after it. | | err:for_loop->ForCommaSeparators | wrong rule: Writes for (int i = 0, i < n, i++). | right rule: The three parts of a for header are separated by semicolons; commas only separate several statements inside the init or the update part. | | err:for_loop->SemicolonAfterIfHeader | wrong rule: if (x > 0); System.out.println("positive"); prints only for positive x. | right rule: The ; ends the if with an empty statement, so the next line always runs. | | err:for_loop->SemicolonAfterLoopHeader | wrong rule: Puts a ; right after for (...) or while (...). | right rule: A ; right after the loop header is a null (empty) loop body, so the statements written after it are not repeated by the loop. | | err:for_loop->WrongIterationCount | wrong rule: Updates the loop counter so that the loop runs the wrong number of times. | right rule: The init, test and update together decide the number of passes; trace them to check the count. | | mis:for_loop->DoubleLoopIndexCount | wrong rule: for (double x = 0.0; x <= 1.0; x += 0.1) runs exactly 11 times. | right rule: Using a double as a for-loop index is legal but bad practice: the number of iterations depends on an equality test between double values, which may not give the result you expect. | | mis:for_loop->FalseLoopRepeatsNextCode | wrong rule: A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats. | right rule: Only the body is repeated; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once. | | mis:for_loop->ForInitRepeats | wrong rule: The initialization of a for loop runs again after a pass of the body. | right rule: The initialization runs exactly once, before the first condition test. | | mis:for_loop->ForIsConditional | wrong rule: The body of a for statement executes at most once. | right rule: The body of a for statement runs once for every pass on which the condition is true, which can be many times. | | mis:for_loop->ForLoopPartSkipped | wrong rule: A pass of a loop may leave out one of its parts (the condition test, the body, the update, or the initialization). | right rule: Each pass of a for loop runs test, then body, then update, every time; the initialization runs once, at the start. | | mis:for_loop->ForUpdateBeforeBody | wrong rule: The update part of a for header (e.g. i = i - 4) runs before the body on each pass, so the first pass already sees the updated value. | right rule: The update runs after the body, before the next condition test; the first pass uses the initial value. | | mis:for_loop->ForWhileNotInterchangeable | wrong rule: Some loops can only be written with for, others only with while. | right rule: Any for loop can be rewritten as a while loop and vice versa; for just packages init, test and update. | | mis:for_loop->IdiomOverridesCode | wrong rule: An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says. | right rule: The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written. | | mis:for_loop->LoopCountIsStatementCount | wrong rule: The repeat count of a counted loop says how many of the body statements are executed. | right rule: The repeat count is how many times the whole body runs; every pass runs all body statements. | | mis:for_loop->LoopHeaderIsEquations | wrong rule: The initialization, condition and update of a for header are equations that all hold at the same time. | right rule: The three header parts are statements run at different moments: init once, then condition test, body, update, repeated. | | mis:for_loop->LoopImpliedByOneTest | wrong rule: Testing one case is enough; Java will repeat the test for the other values by itself. | right rule: A statement runs once each time control reaches it; repeating a test for many values needs a loop. | | mis:for_loop->LoopStepAlwaysOne | wrong rule: A loop variable always goes up or down by 1, whatever the update says (so i = i - 4 is read as i--). | right rule: The loop variable changes exactly as the update expression says (i += 2, i = i - 4, i *= 2, ...). | | mis:for_loop->MissingBraces | wrong rule: Omits braces around a single-statement body of if, for or while. | right rule: Braces are optional for a single-statement body, but using them anyway avoids bugs when statements are added later. | | mis:for_loop->ProgramEndsAfterLoop | wrong rule: When a loop finishes the program ends, so code after the loop never runs. | right rule: When the loop condition becomes false, control continues with the first statement after the loop. | | mis:for_loop->ReturnDoesNotExitLoop | wrong rule: A return inside a loop does not end the loop; it sets a value each pass (the last one is returned) or returns several values. | right rule: When return executes, the method ends at once, so the loop stops on that pass. | | mis:for_loop->SingleIterationInsteadOfLoop | wrong rule: A task that must be repeated is written once, without a loop, as if one pass were enough. | right rule: A step that must happen several times (or an unknown number of times) needs a loop such as while or for; code without a loop runs once. |

the initialization runs once, at the start. | | mis:loop_control->ForUpdateBeforeBody | wrong rule: The update part of a for header (e.g. i = i - 4) runs before the body on each pass, so the first pass already sees the updated value. | right rule: The update runs after the body, before the next condition test; the first pass uses the initial value. | | mis:loop_control->IdiomOverridesCode | wrong rule: An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says. | right rule: The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written. | | mis:loop_control->InfiniteLoopUnnoticed | wrong rule: A while loop always stops on its own, even if nothing in its body can make the condition false. | right rule: A while loop stops only when its condition is false at a check, so if no pass changes the variables in the condition, it never stops. | | mis:loop_control->LoopHeaderIsEquations | wrong rule: The initialization, condition and update of a for header are equations that all hold at the same time. | right rule: The three header parts are statements run at different moments: init once, then condition test, body, update, repeated. | | mis:loop_control->LoopStepAlwaysOne | wrong rule: A loop variable always goes up or down by 1, whatever the update says (so i = i - 4 is read as i--). | right rule: The loop variable changes exactly as the update expression says (i += 2, i = i - 4, i *= 2, ...). | | mis:loop_control->LoopUpdateChangesDirection | wrong rule: The update of the loop variable can change from pass to pass (e.g. switch direction) although the code is the same. | right rule: The update expression is the same on every pass; the loop variable changes by the rule written in the update. | | mis:loop_control->OffByOneBound | wrong rule: i < n and i <= n mean the same, so the loop runs until i equals n and the last pass can use a[n]. | right rule: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) runs n times with i going up to n - 1; with <= it runs n + 1 times and reaches i = n. | | mis:loop_control->PreIncrementBeforeLoop | wrong rule: With ++i in the update of for (int i = s; i < n; ++i), i is increased before the body runs, so the first pass uses s + 1. | right rule: The update runs after each pass of the body, so with either ++i or i++ the first pass uses i = s. |

the rest run once, after it. | | mis:loop_body->ComputerFillsInIntent | wrong rule: The computer fills in omitted steps or values that the programmer meant, e.g. REPEAT 4 [FORWARD 30] draws a square without a turn command. | right rule: The computer executes only what the code states; every needed step and value must be written. | | mis:loop_body->ForLoopPartSkipped | wrong rule: A pass of a loop may leave out one of its parts (the condition test, the body, the update, or the initialization). | right rule: Each pass of a for loop runs test, then body, then update, every time; the initialization runs once, at the start. | | mis:loop_body->IfInLoopUnchecked | wrong rule: An if inside a loop body runs its branch on every pass without testing its condition. | right rule: The if condition is tested again on every pass, with the current values, so the branch runs only on passes where it is true. | | mis:loop_body->LoopBodyAlwaysOnce | wrong rule: The loop body always runs at least once, even if the condition is false at the start. | right rule: A while or for body runs zero times when the condition is false at the start. | | mis:loop_body->LoopBodyStatementOutsideLoop | wrong rule: Some statements inside the braces of a loop body are not repeated; they run once, before or after the loop. | right rule: Every statement inside the loop braces is part of the body and runs on every pass. | | mis:loop_body->LoopCountIsStatementCount | wrong rule: The repeat count of a counted loop says how many of the body statements are executed. | right rule: The repeat count is how many times the whole body runs; every pass runs all body statements. | | mis:loop_body->LoopOutputSameEachPass | wrong rule: A loop prints the same thing on every pass; the changing loop variable does not affect what the body does. | right rule: The body uses the current value of the loop variable, so its output can differ on each pass. | | mis:loop_body->LoopRunsStatementsSeparately | wrong rule: A loop runs its first body statement all N times, then its second body statement all N times. | right rule: Each pass runs the whole body in order, so the body statements interleave: S1, S2, S1, S2, ... | | mis:loop_body->StateChangeIgnoredAcrossPasses | wrong rule: Values changed by one pass of a loop (other than the loop variable) do not affect later passes. | right rule: Each pass starts from the state left by the previous pass, so a change in one pass carries into the next ones. | | mis:loop_body->StatementAfterLoopInBody | wrong rule: A statement written after the loop is repeated with the loop body. | right rule: The body ends at the closing brace (or after its single statement); code after it runs once, after the loop ends. | | mis:loop_body->WhileStopsMidBody | wrong rule: The loop stops the moment the condition becomes false, even in the middle of the body. | right rule: The condition is tested only before each pass, so the whole body finishes before the loop can stop. |

loop_body, level ways: 14 edges offered

Edges offered: | edge | |---| | lvl:loop_body@L0#0 | level L0 way everyday_reading: Folk meaning: an everyday 'repeat this' instruction can be read loosely - a helper fills in missing steps, does each step N times in turn, or stops partway. A Java loop body is exactly the statements inside its braces (or one statement), all executed in order on every pass. | | lvl:loop_body@L0#6 | level L0 way inconsistent_trace: Applies the body rule (LT) unevenly: runs all body statements on some passes but only some on others, includes the statement after the loop on some passes, or uses stale values from the first pass later. (here mixing in: "The loop body always runs at least once, even if the condition is false at the start") | | lvl:loop_body@L1#0 | level L1 way names_the_element: The loop body is the statement block that a loop repeats on each pass. | | lvl:loop_body@L1#1 | level L1 way states_the_rule: The body is the block after the loop header; braces are optional only if it is a single statement, in which case only that one statement is repeated. | | lvl:loop_body@L2#0 | level L2 way line_by_line_trace: On each pass the body's statements run in order, first to last, after a true test (and, in a for loop, before the update); the next pass starts from the state left by this one. | | lvl:loop_body@L2#1 | level L2 way output_prediction: The body's output on each pass depends on the current values, so successive passes can print different lines: TenHellos prints '4th Hello', '5th Hello', ...; the number of executions of each body statement equals the number of passes. | | lvl:loop_body@L2#2 | level L2 way one_step_execution: One pass of the body changes exactly the variables it assigns (e.g. print i and v, double v, increment i) and these changes carry into the next test and pass. | | lvl:loop_body@L3#0 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: The accumulator update (sum += x) is placed inside the body so it runs once per pass, while the accumulator is declared and initialized before the loop. | | lvl:loop_body@L3#1 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: count++ sits inside the body, often under an if, so it runs once on each pass that matches; the counter is declared before the loop. | | lvl:loop_body@L3#2 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: The body is what the while repeats; the condition is tested only between complete executions of it. | | lvl:loop_body@L3#3 | level L3 way purpose_of_the_whole: Plan: the body is the 'process one item / one step' part of a loop plan: each pass performs the same process on a new value (next element, next bet, next term). | | lvl:loop_body@L4#0 | level L4 way predict_a_change: Moving a statement from inside the body to after the loop changes it from running once per pass to once in total (and vice versa); reordering two body statements that share a variable changes the results (e.g. increment before vs after use). | | lvl:loop_body@L4#1 | level L4 way diagnose_an_error: rule broken: Without braces, the body of an if, while or for is exactly one statement; indentation does not add statements to it. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: A braceless header followed by two or more indented statements: only the first is controlled, the others run once, after the if/loop, on every input. | | lvl:loop_body@L4#2 | level L4 way transfer_to_a_new_program: Put inside the body exactly what must happen once per pass; put set-up before the loop and final reporting after it. Always brace a multi-statement body. |
